extracted.intended_audience: physiologists, medical researchers, and members of learned societies (e.g., Royal Society); advanced medical students and clinicians interested in experimental physiology
extracted.subtask_description: A scientific/experimental paper (early 19th-century) analyzing the structure and functions of the nervous system, reporting experiments and drawing conceptual distinctions (e.g., sensorial vs nervous powers). Intended as the concluding observations of an extended inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of nerves into two classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The nerves may be divided into two classes: (1) those which proceed directly from the brain and spinal marrow to the parts they innervate; and (2) those which enter ganglions (ganglionic nerves) that receive fibres from different parts of the brain and spinal marrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author confines the term 'ganglion' to those ganglions receiving nerves from different parts of the nervous system, and 'ganglionic nerve' to nerves which enter or proceed from such ganglions. This classification is presented as important for understanding differing relations to other parts of the nervous system and for avoiding previous imprecision in terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and nature of ganglia
rubrics_metrics.description: Ganglia are of complicated structure: fasciculi of nervous filaments entering a ganglion divide into smaller fasciculi, cross and intersect, and then reunite into larger bundles; every fasciculus passing through a ganglion; and between fibres is a soft grayish or yellowish substance of unknown nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper quotes Scarpa and other anatomists (and unpublished Brodie lectures) as summarizing current knowledge of ganglionic structure. The description underpins later functional inferences (mixing/blending of fibres explains shared influence). The nature of the interstitial substance is discussed as uncertain (opinions: cineritious-like vs soft cellular/mucilaginous or oily in fat subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ganglionic nerves anastomose and widely distribute influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ganglionic nerves more freely anastomose (interconnect) than nerves proceeding directly from brain and spinal marrow; they unite nerves arising from many parts and send influence to vital organs (thoracic and abdominal viscera, vessels, capillaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This perpetual intertwining is argued to be purposeful: because ganglionic nerves arise from many parts of brain/spinal marrow, vital organs receive the influence of every part. The paper cites experiments showing heart and vessels can be influenced by stimuli applied to many parts of brain/spinal marrow, and even capillary action can be altered by such stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional role of ganglionic connectivity for secretory and structural processes
rubrics_metrics.description: By means of the ganglionic system, the influence of every part of the brain and spinal marrow is bestowed on secreting surfaces and organs that regulate fluid supply; this combined influence is necessary for secretion and the processes that maintain healthy tissue structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that secretion depends on both nervous influence and an appropriately supplied blood (sanguiferous system), so vascular supply must be regulated under the same laws. Experiments (cited from the author's treatises and Philosophical Transactions) are referenced as evidence that removal of neurological influence deranges secretory function and tissue maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensorial and nervous powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensorial (sensorial power) is a principle of action distinct from the nervous power properly so called; the sensorial power resides chiefly in the brain, while the nervous power resides equally in brain and spinal marrow and can act independently of the sensorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction is supported by experiments (e.g., Le Gallois and the author's own) showing that the spinal marrow can perform functions of the nervous power independently. The sensorial functions (sensation and volition) are said to cease earlier in dying, while many nervous functions may persist; this conceptual split is used to analyze differing phenomena (e.g., post-mortem excitability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue of 'nervous functions' properly so called
rubrics_metrics.description: The nervous functions properly so called include: (1) excitement of muscles of voluntary motion (allowing sensorial power to act through them); (2) occasional excitement of muscles of involuntary motion (e.g., under passions); (3) causing evolution of caloric from the blood (maintaining animal temperature); (4) forming various secreted fluids from the blood; and (5) supporting other assimilating processes preserving tissue structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes the first function is universally acknowledged but debates remain about mechanism (stimulus vs intrinsic muscle power). Experimental references (own treatise, others) are supplied to classify these as functions of the nervous power. The list frames subsequent experimental claims about independence from sensorial power and substitutability by external agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscle power is intrinsic; nerves act as stimulus
rubrics_metrics.description: Muscular power (excitability) belongs to the muscle itself and is independent of the nervous power; the nervous system acts as a stimulus rather than the source of muscular power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by experiments: muscles with divided nerves sustained action from artificial stimuli longer than those with intact nerves (exposure to both nervous power and artificial stimulus weakens endurance). The longstanding debate (Haller vs opponents) is discussed and the author's experiments are offered as decisive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nervous functions persist after loss of sensorial power (post-sensorial continuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the sensorial functions (sensation and volition) cease (e.g., at death), many nervous functions still continue for some time: nerves can still excite voluntary muscles, involuntary muscles, evolve caloric, form secreted fluids, and support structural processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites multiple experiments (own treatises and Philosophical Transactions) showing post-mortem or post-sensorial continuation: e.g., stimulation of nerves after 'death' elicits muscle contraction; some gastric secretion occurs after death; dividing certain nerves immediately after death can derange lung structure—supporting continuation of nervous functions independent of sensorial faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nervous power transferable through non-nervous conductors
rubrics_metrics.description: The nervous power can be made to pass through substances other than the nerves, demonstrating its existence independent of nervous tissue, and thereby suggesting it is an agent employed by vital powers rather than unique to living organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author reports experiments (published 1822; repeated by Brechet et al.) showing transmission of the nervous agent through other conductors. This empirical result is used as a basis for arguing that the nervous agent is not exclusive to living tissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galvanism as a substitute for nervous power
rubrics_metrics.description: Galvanism (electrical/galvanic stimulation) can substitute for the nervous power in both simple and complex functions: exciting muscles, causing caloric evolution, forming secreted fluids, and supporting processes maintaining body structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments (Philosophical Transactions 1822, 1828; repeated by Abel, Brechet, others) are cited showing galvanism replicates many nervous functions. The author poses the question of how far these facts support the identity of nervous power with galvanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration depends on sensorial, nervous, and muscular powers jointly
rubrics_metrics.description: Respiration partakes of sensorial, nervous, and muscular powers; loss of the sensorial power leads to cessation of respiration because breathing (expansion of chest) is an act of volition induced by sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues muscles of respiration are muscles of voluntary motion (though habit makes the act unconscious); respiration requires periodic volitional impulses (sensation of need for fresh air). Thus when sensorial functions are removed, respiration stops and secondary failure of circulation/tissue function follows, explaining rapid death after loss of sensorial power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscles of respiration are voluntary acts rendered habitual
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of expanding the chest (inspiration) is an act of volition; it is ordinarily unconscious due to habit and the slightness of the inducing sensation, but it remains a voluntary act subject to will when attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: directing attention to breathing makes the sensation and volitional control evident; comparison with other habitual voluntary acts (walking, playing instrument). Clinical observations (apoplexy, sleep) are used to illustrate that respiration is governed by volition through the sensorium until insensibility prevents it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and manner in which functions cease in death
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in cases of instantaneous destruction by sudden extreme nervous injury, sensorial functions cease first in the dying process, while other nervous and muscular functions persist longer and fail subsequently as respiration and circulation deteriorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper traces the cascade: loss of respiration leads to pulmonary and cardiac failure (right heart congestion, left-heart underfilling), arterial failure of supplying assimilative fluids, and eventual failure of nervous and muscular solids. Empirical observations and experiments are invoked to support this sequence.
